```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
                      fig.height = 5, dpi = 72)
```

The spatial point pattern test asks whether two sets of events, for example
residential burglaries in two different years, are distributed the same way
across a set of areal units. `sppt()` answers that unit by unit, and then
summarises the whole map.

```{r}
library(sppt)
```

## Getting started

The package includes residential (`BNER`) and commercial (`BNEC`) burglary
counts for Vancouver from 2003 to 2025, in 127 census tracts
(`vancouver_ct`) and 1,016 dissemination areas (`vancouver_da`).

To compare residential burglary in 2003 (the base) with 2025 (the test), name
the identifier column and the two count columns. `alpha = 0.05` is the
default and is shown here for clarity.

```{r quick}
res <- sppt(
  data      = vancouver_ct,
  group_col = "id",
  count_col = c("BNER2003", "BNER2025"),
  B         = 999,
  alpha     = 0.05,
  seed      = 42,
  create_maps = FALSE
)
```

The console report gives:

* **lambda_min**, the mean number of events per unit in the rarer pattern,
  which governs power, and the decision tier that follows from it;
* the **robust S index**, the share of units (not empty in both years) whose
  share of events did not change significantly;
* the **sameness test**, which asks whether that S index is lower than two
  realisations of one process would give;
* **S_D**, the degree of similarity: the share of each pattern already in
  place once only the flagged units are allowed to differ, with the index of
  dissimilarity D and the number of events that would have to move;
* the **arrangement test**, Moran's I on the signed evidence surface, which
  asks whether the differences cluster in space;
* the **confidence tiers** of the flagged units (core, edge, outside);
* a **two-way verdict** that reads the count and arrangement results
  together.

`summary()` repeats the key results at any time.

```{r}
summary(res)
```

Each unit gets a p-value and a direction: 1 where the test pattern has the
larger share, -1 where the base has, and 0 where the difference is not
significant.

```{r}
table(res$sig_pvalue_dir, useNA = "ifany")
```

The p-value is the bounded Monte Carlo form $p = (1 + r)/(B + 1)$, so it is
never exactly zero; with `B = 999` the smallest possible value is 0.001.
The default, `B = "auto"`, uses 4999 replicates at `alpha = 0.05`, more at
smaller `alpha` or under a correction.

## Sameness and degree of similarity

S tests sameness: is S lower than the 1 - alpha that two realisations of one
process give? It does not say how far apart two different patterns are. S_D
does, in events: `sppt_similarity()` returns it with the index of
dissimilarity D.

```{r similarity}
sppt_similarity(res)
```

Where power is limited many real differences are not flagged and S_D
overstates similarity, so `share_d_flagged` reports how much of D the flagged
units hold. Over the flagged units the shares where each pattern is higher
need not balance, so `share_to_move`, the larger of `flagged_test_higher` and
`flagged_base_higher`, is the exact share that would have to move; 1 - S_D
approximates it from below.

## Testing against a random distribution

Give a single column, or a column and `"random"`, to ask how far one pattern
is from random and where it differs. The random distribution spreads the
column's own total over the units in proportion to their exposure: area for
polygons, length for lines such as street segments. `random_by = "units"`
gives every unit equal probability, and naming a column (population, say)
uses it as the exposure.

```{r random}
res_r <- sppt(vancouver_ct, group_col = "id", count_col = "BNER2021",
              B = 999, seed = 42, verbose = FALSE, create_maps = FALSE)
sppt_similarity(res_r)
```

Positive differences mark tracts with more residential burglary than a random
allocation in proportion to area would give. Here D measures how concentrated
burglary is relative to land area, a Hoover-type index of concentration.

## Reading the map at fine scales

At census tracts most flagged units are trustworthy individually. At finer
units, power falls and false discoveries rise, but the errors behave
differently: false positives are scattered, while genuine differences hold
together. Two tools use that.

**Confidence tiers.** Each flagged unit is placed in a tier: *core* if it
lies inside a local Moran cluster of the same direction, *edge* if it
borders a core unit with the same sign, and *outside* otherwise. All three
are significant at `alpha`; the tiers rank how much to trust them.

```{r tiers}
res_da <- sppt(vancouver_da, group_col = "id",
               count_col = c("BNER2021", "BNEC2021"),
               B = 999, seed = 42, verbose = FALSE, create_maps = FALSE)
table(res_da$confidence_tier, res_da$sig_pvalue_dir)
```

```{r tier-map, fig.height = 6}
plot(res_da, "tiers")
```

**Cluster test.** `sppt_clusters()` groups flagged units into clusters and
compares their sizes with the clusters that false positives alone form on
the same map. A cluster above the ceiling is a pattern chance is unlikely to
produce, even where its individual units are uncertain.

```{r clusters}
sppt_clusters(res_da, rule = "one_gap", nsim = 499, seed = 1)
```

## Maps

With `create_maps = TRUE` (the default), `sppt()` prints a difference map, a
significance map and, with the arrangement test, a confidence tier map, and
stores them on the result. `sppt_map()` and `plot()` redraw them, with the
legend, north arrow and scale bar wherever suits your study area.

```{r map}
sppt_map(res, "pvalue")
```

```{r map-custom}
sppt_map(res, "pvalue", legend_position = "right",
         north_arrow = "tl", scale_bar = "br", title = FALSE)
```

The maps are ordinary `ggplot` objects, so anything else can be changed by
adding to them, for example
`sppt_map(res, "difference") + ggplot2::scale_fill_viridis_c()`.

## Saving results

Nothing is written to disk unless you ask. To save the maps and the result,
name a directory:

```{r export, eval = FALSE}
res <- sppt(vancouver_ct, group_col = "id",
            count_col = c("BNER2003", "BNER2025"),
            export_maps = TRUE, export_results = TRUE,
            export_format = "gpkg", export_dir = "sppt_output")
```

`export_format = "rds"` keeps the summary and the maps with the data;
`readRDS()` restores everything, and `summary()` and `sppt_map()` work on the
reloaded object. The result is also an ordinary `sf` object, so
`sf::st_write()` works on it directly.

## All options

The call below lists every argument with its default value.

```{r all-options, eval = FALSE}
res <- sppt(
  data               = vancouver_ct,
  group_col          = "id",
  count_col          = c("BNER2003", "BNER2025"), # base, then test
  B                  = "auto",  # replicates, chosen from alpha and correction
  seed               = NULL,    # set for reproducible results
  alpha              = 0.05,    # unit-level significance level
  calculate_pvalues  = TRUE,    # bootstrap p-values
  sameness_tau       = 0.05,    # significance level of the sameness test
  arrangement        = TRUE,    # Moran's I on the signed evidence surface
  nsim_moran         = 999,     # permutations for global Moran's I
  correction         = "none",  # or "BY", "BH", "bonferroni", ...
  calculate_ci       = FALSE,   # also compute marginal CI overlap (2009)
  conf_level         = 0.85,    # CI level; about alpha = 0.05
  fix_base           = FALSE,   # TRUE = do not bootstrap the base pattern
  use_percentages    = TRUE,    # percentages (0-100) rather than proportions
  verbose            = TRUE,    # print the console report
  create_maps        = TRUE,    # build, print and store the maps
  map_crs            = NULL,    # CRS for the maps; NULL keeps that of data
  export_maps        = FALSE,   # save maps as PNG in export_dir
  export_dir         = NULL,    # required for any export
  map_dpi            = 300,     # resolution of exported maps
  export_results     = FALSE,   # save the result
  export_format      = "gpkg",  # gpkg, shp, csv, txt or rds
  export_results_dir = NULL     # defaults to export_dir
)
```

### Confidence interval overlap

The original test (Andresen 2009) compared bootstrap confidence intervals.
`calculate_ci = TRUE` adds that method alongside the p-values, using the same
bootstrap replicates. Two marginal intervals at the default
`conf_level = 0.85` fail to overlap when the difference exceeds about 2.04
standard errors, which corresponds to a two-sample test at about
`alpha = 0.05`; 0.95 reproduces the original, more conservative analysis.

### Multiple testing corrections

None is applied by default. At fine scales corrections remove most of the
power, and at coarse scales a stricter `alpha` does much the same job. Where
a list of units with controlled error is wanted, `correction = "BY"` controls
the false discovery rate under any dependence between units. Raw p-values
stay in `pvalue`, adjusted ones go in `pvalue_adj`, and the sameness test is
not reported, because chance flags are no longer binomial with rate `alpha`.

A correction needs many replicates: the smallest attainable p-value,
1/(B + 1), must survive it. `B = "auto"` takes care of this, and computes
large numbers of replicates in blocks so that memory stays modest.

### Fixed base

`fix_base = TRUE` treats the base pattern as known rather than sampled. That
suits a comparison against a theoretical or population distribution, but the
test is then asymmetric, and the sameness test is not reported.

## References

Andresen, M.A. (2009). Testing for similarity in area-based spatial patterns:
A nonparametric Monte Carlo approach. *Applied Geography*, 29(3), 333-345.
<doi:10.1016/j.apgeog.2008.12.004>

Andresen, M.A. (2016). An area-based nonparametric spatial point pattern
test: The test, its applications, and the future. *Methodological
Innovations*, 9, Article 12. <doi:10.1177/2059799116630659>
